ui.tagline: Terraform on AWS with CI gates, FinOps and failure scenarios. Runs locally on an emulator: no cloud account, no cost.
ui.pipeline_intro: Every button runs the same make targets that CI runs. The apply stage waits for a manual approval, like a protected environment in GitHub Actions.
ui.approval_text: All gates passed. Review the plan log above, then approve or reject the apply.

ui.not_applied: Nothing is applied yet. Run the pipeline first.
ui.map_intro: Drawn from terraform show -json (the state), plus the live security group rules read from the emulator API.
ui.state_backend_text: S3 bucket (versioned, SSE) + DynamoDB lock table
ui.lab_intro: Each scenario injects one real fault and shows which control stops it. Plan-time faults are blocked before anything is applied; runtime faults change the emulator behind Terraform's back.

missing-route.title: Missing route
missing-route.story: The NAT gateway is disabled to save money. The app tier silently loses its default route and its outbound access.

card.context: App subnets reach the internet only through a NAT gateway. Removing the NAT also removes their 0.0.0.0/0 route, and nothing fails until an application times out.
card.automated: A plan rule: every route table tagged Tier=public or Tier=app must have a default route; Tier=data must have none.
card.pipeline: make policy reads the plan JSON right after terraform plan and fails the run before the approval step.
card.before: Before: found after apply, by an application that cannot reach its dependencies.
card.risks: The rule depends on the Tier tag, so a route table without a valid tag fails the rule instead of being skipped.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto). Not executed in a real AWS account.

open-security-group.title: Open security group
open-security-group.story: A temporary rule opens the database port to 0.0.0.0/0 so someone can debug from home.

card.context: The database security group should accept connections from the app tier only. A wide-open rule is the classic shortcut that never gets removed.
card.automated: A custom Checkov policy (CKV2_LAB_1) rejects any security group ingress from 0.0.0.0/0, on top of the built-in checks.
card.pipeline: make scan runs Checkov on the resolved plan, so the value is checked even when it arrives through a variable.
card.before: Before: depends on a reviewer noticing one CIDR in a diff.
card.risks: Skipped checks are listed in .checkov.yaml, each with its reason. A new skip is visible in code review.
card.validated: Scan executed locally on the plan. Not executed in a real AWS account.

costly-resource.title: Forgotten costly resource
costly-resource.story: A load test sized the database up to db.r6g.xlarge Multi-AZ and nobody sized it back down.

card.context: Instance class and Multi-AZ are one-line changes that multiply the bill. They pass every functional test.
card.automated: An offline estimate per resource from the plan, compared with a monthly budget. In CI, Infracost can replace the reference price table.
card.pipeline: make cost prints the estimate and fails when the total is over BUDGET (100 USD/month in the lab).
card.before: Before: found on the invoice, weeks later.
card.risks: Prices are a labelled reference snapshot (finops/prices.json), not a quote. Unknown instance classes are flagged, never priced as zero. Data transfer is not estimated.
card.validated: Estimate executed locally on the plan with reference list prices. Infracost was not run.

state-lock.title: Stale state lock
state-lock.story: A pipeline job is cancelled in the middle of an apply and never releases its lock. Every later run is blocked.

card.context: The DynamoDB lock prevents two runs from writing the same state. A killed job leaves the lock behind.
card.automated: Every plan and apply uses the remote backend with locking and -lock-timeout=0s, so a held lock fails fast with the lock ID and owner.
card.pipeline: The plan stage fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock'. After confirming the owner is dead, make unlock ID=<id> releases it.
card.before: Before (local state, no lock): two concurrent applies can corrupt the state.
card.risks: force-unlock on a lock that is still alive causes exactly the corruption the lock prevents: confirm the owner first. The lab simulates the killed job by writing the lock item directly.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto S3 + DynamoDB). Not executed in a real AWS account.

drift.title: Drift
drift.story: Someone adds an ingress rule to the database security group by hand, outside Terraform.

card.context: Manual changes make the real infrastructure differ from the code. The next apply may revert them, or worse, they stay unnoticed.
card.automated: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode as a drift check. Security group rules are inline, so Terraform owns the whole rule set and sees rules it did not create.
card.pipeline: make drift fails with DRIFT DETECTED and shows the diff. The fix is a normal plan + apply, which removes the manual rule.
card.before: Before: the rule is found in an audit, or never.
card.risks: Only attributes Terraform manages are compared. With standalone rule resources, a rule added by hand would not be detected.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto). Not executed in a real AWS account.

dirty-destroy.title: Dirty destroy
dirty-destroy.story: A security group and a network interface are created by hand inside the VPC. They are not in the state.

card.context: On AWS, resources created outside Terraform block the VPC deletion with DependencyViolation, or survive the destroy and keep costing money.
card.automated: orphan-check lists everything in the account that is not in the Terraform state, and whether it carries the ManagedBy tag.
card.pipeline: make orphan-check runs after every destroy and fails when anything is left. It can also run on a schedule.
card.before: Before: leftovers are found by reading the console region by region.
card.risks: The check covers the resource types this lab creates, not every AWS service. The emulator does not enforce DependencyViolation, so the lab shows the detection, not the failed destroy.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto). Not executed in a real AWS account.

secret-leak.title: Secret leak
secret-leak.story: A deploy.env file with an AWS access key is about to be committed.

card.context: A key pushed to a repository must be treated as compromised, even if the commit is removed later.
card.automated: gitleaks scans the working tree in the pipeline. The lab generates a random fake key at runtime, so the repository never contains one.
card.pipeline: make secrets fails with 'leaks found' and the file and line, with the value redacted.
card.before: Before: the key is found by whoever scans public repositories first.
card.risks: Detection is pattern-based: unusual secret formats need custom rules. Removing the file is not enough, the key must be revoked.
card.validated: Scan executed locally. The pipeline uses OIDC roles in the documented cloud setup, so no long-lived key exists to leak.

validation: VPC, subnets, routes, NAT gateway, flow logs
RDS instance, subnet group, security group
API mock: no database engine runs
RDS parameter group values (rds.force_ssl) and Performance Insights
The emulator does not keep them
Alarms never fire: the emulator has no metrics
Remote state in S3 (versioning, SSE) with DynamoDB lock
TLS-only bucket policy on the state bucket
Checkov, route and tag policy, cost gate, gitleaks
Run on the plan inside the lab container
Configured in the image and Makefile
Needs an API key; the lab uses the offline price table
Anything in a real AWS account
Nothing was executed in a real account
adrs: LocalStack now requires an account and auth token. moto is open source, needs no account and covers every service used here.
Newer provider versions (6.40 and 6.73 were tested) use a CloudWatch wire protocol that moto 5.2.5 does not answer. 6.20.0 is the newest version verified to work.
Gates run on the plan JSON, not on raw HCL
Variables are already resolved in the plan, so a bad value passed by tfvars is caught. One file feeds Checkov, the policy and the cost gate.
One Makefile for people, CI and the UI
What the UI shows is exactly what CI runs. There is no second implementation to drift.
Routes as separate resources, security group rules inline
A removed inline route block is ignored by the provider. Inline security group rules give Terraform exclusive ownership, which is what detects manual rules.

Terraform now prefers use_lockfile (native S3 locking). The table is kept because many existing estates still use it and it makes the stale-lock scenario visible. Migration is a one-line backend change.
A filesystem mirror in the image means make up needs no registry access at runtime, and the provider version cannot float.
UI in plain HTML and JavaScript, docs inside the UI
No build step, no CDN, works offline. Easy to read from top to bottom.
lessons: A TLS-only bucket policy locks an HTTP emulator out of its own state bucket. The policy is validated by plan and scan only.
Deleting an inline route block does not delete the route. The first version of the missing-route scenario passed the gate for that reason.
The emulator drops RDS parameter values and Performance Insights, which shows as permanent drift. The lab passes none there and keeps the secure defaults for real accounts.
Creating the RDS instance takes about 80 seconds even on the emulator, because the provider waits and polls. Measured on this lab.
Checkov tries to download guidelines on every run. --skip-download keeps it offline.
After a destroy the emulator keeps the NAT gateway's network interface in a VPC that no longer exists. orphan-check ignores interfaces without a VPC and documents why.
The dependency lock file is not committed: hashes for every platform cannot be generated offline. The provider version is pinned exactly instead.
Cost: the lab costs nothing. By the reference list prices, the baseline would cost about 55 USD/month on AWS, and the NAT gateway is the largest line.
